text: The last lesson argued that qubit count, fidelity, and connectivity all matter together, not separately — which raises an obvious question: can you fold them into one number? Several vendors have tried. This lesson covers the best-known attempt, and teaches you to stay skeptical of all of them.

Quantum Volume, introduced by IBM, stops asking how many qubits a chip has and instead asks what's the largest random square circuit this chip can run and still trust the answer — a circuit using n qubits arranged in n layers of random two-qubit operations. The benchmark finds the largest n for which the device passes reliably, then converts that into a score with QV equals 2 to the n. If the largest passing circuit is n equals 6, QV is 64; n equals 7 gives QV of 128. That doubling is intentional — it reflects how quickly circuits get harder to run correctly as both width and depth grow together, so a jump from 64 to 128 represents a real, nontrivial capability increase, not a small increment. A device can't game this by adding qubits that don't connect well or that compound too much error, because the test circuits grow in depth at the same rate they grow in width.

QV is still a single aggregate number, and aggregating always loses information. It uses one specific family of random circuits, so it measures that statistical profile, not necessarily how a device handles your specific structured algorithm. It says nothing about raw speed — how long the device actually takes to run those circuits. And because the test circuits are square, it doesn't directly tell you how a device handles circuits that are much wider than deep, or much deeper than wide, both common in real algorithms.

Other composite benchmarks exist, and you should expect to see them cited, especially by vendors whose devices score well on them. CLOPS, Circuit Layer Operations Per Second, measures speed, which QV doesn't capture. Algorithmic qubits, promoted by some trapped-ion vendors, attempts to express how many good-enough qubits a device effectively provides once realistic error rates are accounted for. The existence of multiple competing metrics is itself a lesson: a benchmark isn't a neutral law of physics, it's a specific test with specific assumptions, and a vendor whose architecture happens to score well on one particular benchmark has every incentive to promote exactly that one.

Next lesson puts this discipline to work by walking through how you'd actually choose hardware for a specific, realistic workload — using benchmarks as one input among several, never as the whole answer.
